use_cases.name: Workflow automation with n8n, self-hosted
use_cases.what_it_is: n8n is a visual workflow automation server: you draw a workflow on a canvas, it runs on your machine, and it starts from a webhook, a schedule, a chat message or an app event. Self-hosted means you run the server, its database and its upgrades.

minimum.note: n8n publishes Cloud plan limits rather than a self-host floor: Starter is 640 MiB RAM and 10 millicore of burstable CPU, and the software alone averages about 180 MiB. It publishes no self-host CPU or disk floor; Cloud gives each instance up to 100 GB. 1 vCPU is the smallest practical allocation, not a vendor figure.

recommended.note: 4 GiB matches n8n's Enterprise Cloud allowance and Lizard's template limit, which Lizard says is not a measured recommendation. 20 GiB covers the database, execution history and binary data for a small instance.

use_cases.always_on_detail: Yes for webhooks and schedules. n8n registers a production webhook only while the workflow is published and the instance is running, and the Schedule Trigger fires from the instance's own timer. A sleeping machine receives neither. A workflow that is only ever started by hand can live on a machine that sleeps.
use_cases.inbound: Inbound HTTPS to the editor and to /webhook/* paths; internal timer for Schedule Trigger; outbound calls to the apps and models each workflow uses.
persists: The n8n database: workflows, credentials, execution history (SQLite by default, PostgreSQL recommended)
N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY, without which stored credentials cannot be decrypted
Binary data, if workflows handle files and storage is set to filesystem or S3
~/.n8n for the encryption key, config and local files when the container has no volume
use_cases.needs_docker: yes for the documented install; npm is the alternative

use_cases.name: A Discord or Slack bot backed by an LLM
use_cases.what_it_is: A small long-running program that holds a connection to Discord or Slack, receives messages, calls a model, and replies in the channel. Discord bots normally hold a persistent WebSocket to Discord's gateway; Slack apps can either hold a WebSocket (Socket Mode) or receive each event over HTTPS.

minimum.note: No chat platform publishes a server sizing floor for bots. 1 vCPU / 1 GiB / 5 GiB is the smallest shape that runs Node or Python, a SQLite history and a socket client. Battleships models the same job at 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 20 GiB.

recommended.note: 2 GiB covers the runtime, a SQLite or small Postgres client and one model call at a time; 20 GiB covers logs, history and snapshots. Battleships' always-on preset uses 4 GiB.

use_cases.always_on_detail: Yes for a Discord gateway bot and for a Slack Socket Mode app: both hold an outbound WebSocket, and a sleeping machine drops it. A Slack app that uses a public Request URL only needs to be awake when a message arrives, so it can sleep if the host wakes on inbound HTTP. Discord slash-command bots can also use an Interactions Endpoint URL instead of the gateway.
use_cases.inbound: Persistent outbound WebSocket to Discord's gateway or Slack's Socket Mode endpoint; alternatively inbound HTTPS to a Discord Interactions Endpoint URL or a Slack Request URL.
persists: The bot token and any app-level token (Slack)
Conversation history and per-user memory (SQLite or Postgres)
Any prompt/config files and the code itself
Optionally a vector index or cache for retrieval
use_cases.needs_database: recommended for history; SQLite is enough for one replica
official_backends: Any Linux host with outbound HTTPS

use_cases.name: Hosting a remote MCP server over HTTP
use_cases.what_it_is: An MCP server exposes tools, prompts or resources to an AI client over the Model Context Protocol. A remote one speaks Streamable HTTP at a public HTTPS URL, so Claude, Claude Code or another client can connect to it without running anything locally.

minimum.note: No vendor publishes an MCP server floor. A stateless server is a small HTTP process; 512 MiB and 1 GiB of disk cover the runtime and logs. Cloudflare's Workers free plan shows the low end: 10 ms of CPU per invocation.

recommended.note: A small HTTP process plus logs and an optional session store. Heavy tools (code execution, browser) should be sized like the workload they run.

use_cases.always_on_detail: Yes for a normal remote URL: the client connects when it wants a tool, and the server must answer. A host that sleeps can still work if it wakes on the inbound request, at the cost of a cold start on the first call after idle.
use_cases.inbound: Inbound HTTPS to a single MCP endpoint, using POST for JSON-RPC messages and optionally GET for a server-to-client stream.
persists: Usually nothing: a stateless server keeps no state between requests
OAuth signing keys, client registrations and token signing material, if you use OAuth
A session map, if the server issues MCP session IDs
The data the tools read, which normally lives in an external database, not on the server
use_cases.needs_browser: no, unless a tool drives one
use_cases.needs_database: optional; only if a tool needs one
official_backends: Any sandbox with a public port or custom domain

battleships.name: Always-on AI employees
battleships.description: Assistant agents that each live on their own machine all the time (one per employee or customer, like OpenClaw or Hermes): they keep their memory and files, hold logins to your tools, answer messages, run scheduled jobs and use a browser.
battleships.note: No MCP preset exists. `employees` is the nearest always-on shape, but it models an agent doing work, not a thin HTTP adapter. Use it as an upper bound only.

proposed_workload.reasoning: A stateless MCP server is a small HTTP process. 1 vCPU / 1 GiB / 10 GiB covers the runtime, logs and an optional session store. 730 hours if the URL must always answer; a host that wakes on inbound HTTP can bill only the calls instead. 2% CPU is an estimate below Battleships' always-on 5.8%, because the server only adapts tool calls.
